The Story of Vashishth the Ascetic

I bow to Lord Jinendra, who is free from the eighteen faults — hunger, thirst, disease, sorrow, birth, death, fear, delusion, anxiety, attachment, aversion, and more — and I write the story of Vashishth the ascetic.

Ugrasen was king of Mathura, and his queen was Revati, whom he loved dearly. In Mathura lived a merchant named Jindatt, who had a maidservant named Priyangulata. On the banks of the Yamuna lived an ascetic named Vashishth, who bathed daily and practised the austerity of the five fires. People considered him a great ascetic and served him with devotion. Truly, ignorant people follow what they see without understanding.

Even the maidservants who came to draw water from the well would circumambulate the ascetic with great reverence, touch his feet, and serve him before going home. Most followed this practice. But Priyangulata did not. She found these practices distasteful, for she had served in a Jain household since childhood and knew the true path of dharma. The other maidservants disapproved of her stubbornness, and one day they took her by force to the ascetic and pressed her head to his feet against her will.

Priyangulata could not contain herself. She said, "Even if I must bow to someone, why not bow to a fisherman? He is far better than this one." Hearing his own servant girl's criticism, the ascetic was furious. He scolded the maidservants who had forced Priyangulata to bow. The maidservants, seeing his angry red eyes, fled immediately. But the ascetic's wrath was not yet quenched.

He went to King Ugrasen and complained, "Maharaj, Jindatt's maidservant called me a fisherman and insulted me greatly. What right did she have to speak ill of a holy man?" The king, who also disapproved of a servant girl insulting a sage of another tradition, summoned Jindatt and asked him about it. Jindatt replied, "Maharaj, if this man practises austerity, then he is indeed an ascetic — who disputes that? But I never called him a fisherman." And truly, Jindatt had said nothing of the sort.

The king investigated and found that Jindatt was innocent. The ascetic's complaint was baseless — he had been insulted by a maidservant, not by the merchant. The king dismissed the case, and the ascetic returned home in shame.

This story teaches that true spirituality is not measured by outward displays of austerity but by inner purity and freedom from passion. The ascetic who practises the five fires may appear holy, but when his ego is wounded by a servant girl's words, his anger reveals his true state. A true sage remains equanimous in the face of praise or blame, honour or dishonour. The Jain tradition values such inner peace above all external rites.
